Sure. 4-7 metres sounds close (especially if GPS accuracy was about 4 m). How long were the transects and how large are the raccoon home ranges? The distance off the line may be ignorable relative to both the scale of raccoon movements and the length of transect. Then you have the option of the 'transect' detector type in 'secr', possibly discretized as a large number of notional point detectors. Sorry to keep asking, I'm still trying to understand.

A more fundamental issue is that capture-resight data are not capture-recapture data. Capture-resight data can be handled in recent versions of 'secr', and this capability is much improved in the next release, coming perhaps in a couple of months.However, that does not handle _transect_ capture-resight data as such (you would need to use the discretization trick).

Murray

messages.subject_clean: Animals detected outside the transect for the SECR packet
messages.body_plain:
It's good to simulate some data. I guess the raccoon density is about 0.4/ha (I could be very wrong!). The code below generates a transect, simulates some capture-recapture data and estimates density from the discretized transect. I haven't thought about the mark-resight nature of the data (I would have to ask more questions!).

library(secr)

## generate transect
x <- seq(0, pi*2, length = 50)
temptrans <- make.transect(x = x*132, y = sin(x)*132, exclusive = FALSE)
transectlength(temptrans)

## simulated population and sightings
pop <- sim.popn(temptrans, D = 0.4, buffer = 400)
tempcapt <- sim.capthist(temptrans, popn = pop, detectfn = 'HHN', detectpar =
                             list(lambda0 = 0.5, sigma = 100), noccasions=15)
session(tempcapt) <- 'Full data - locations along transect'

## discretize transect data at 20 metre spacing
CH <- discretize(tempcapt, spacing = 20)
session(CH) <- 'Discretized 20-m sections'

par(mfrow=c(2,1), mar=c(0,1,4,1))

plot(temptrans)
plot(pop, add=TRUE)
plot(tempcapt, add = TRUE, tracks = TRUE)

plot(CH, tracks = TRUE)
plot(pop, add=TRUE)

predict(secr.fit(CH, detectfn = 'HHN', buffer=400))

Hi all -

I am running into an issue with memory limits and I cannot figure out why.  The dataset is from bear rub trees.  There are ~900 trap locations and 3 sampling occasions.  All the files look ok, and a series of models with default covariates (e.g. bk, T, etc.) have all run successfully.  I am now trying to add site-specific covariates to g0 and sigma.  These are stored in the trap file and include things such as canopy cover and terrain ruggedness.  An example of model structure is:

D~1, g0~bk+cc, sigma~1 where cc is canopy cover

I get the following error message when running female models:
Error: cannot allocate vector of size 7.8 Gb

For males the error is:
Error: cannot allocate vector of size 14.8 Gb

I have never run into this error before, even when running more complex models on larger data sets.  My computer has 12GB of RAM.

Things I have tried:
-restarting my computer
-restarting R
-reinstalling R and secr
-remaking and error checking my trap file
-remaking and error checking my capthist file
-checking to make sure the covariates are seen as numeric rather than factors
-using memory.limit() - this briefly worked when I set memory.limit(size = 200,000), but ran painfully slow and ultimately made my computer crash
-using a different computer

All of my files appear to be ok. I cannot find anything unusual, and as I've mentioned I've remade them a few different times now.

I get the same error message regardless of the spatial covariate, and regardless of whether it is attached to g0 or sigma.  I have run these exact models with the same covariates on a different data set (110 traps, 6 sampling occasions), and did not have any issues.

I'm not sure what else to try.  I'd appreciate any suggestions folks might have.

Thank you!
Andrea

messages.body_plain:
This is a recurring problem, so I'm thinking of adding a repair function 'shareFactorLevels'  to the next release. If you're in a hurry then copy and paste from here. Usage (no example yet) is msCH <- shareFactorLevels(msCH).
Murray

shareFactorLevels <- function (object, columns = NULL) {
    if (ms(object)) {
        if (!is.null(covariates(object))) {
            df <- do.call(rbind, covariates(object))
            if (is.null(columns)) columns <- 1:ncol(df)
            for (i in columns) {
                if (is.factor(df[,i])) {
                    levelsi <- levels(df[,i])
                    for (sess in 1:length(object)) {
                        covariates(object[[sess]])[,i] <-
                            factor(covariates(object[[sess]])[,i],
                                   levels = levelsi)
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    object
}

shareFactorLevelsR Documentation
Fix Inconsistent Covariates
Description

Factor covariates can give trouble in multi-session models if the levels differ among sessions. A warning is provided by verify.capthist. This function forces factor covariates to use the same levels.
Usage
shareFactorLevels(object, columns = NULL)

Arguments
object

multi-session capthist object or list of traps or mask objects
columns

indices of columns to fix (default all)
Details

Factor-valued covariates are coerced to use the same set of levels for each session of a multi-session capthist object or each component of a list of traps or masks. The combined level set is the union of all levels in separate sessions. The order of levels follows the default in factor (alphabetical).
Value

An object of the same class as input.
See Also

verify.capthist

Hi JMJ

I am not optimistic that there is an easy solution. The error message is fairly generic, just indicating that likelihood maximisation crashed. There could be (i) problems in the software itself (the mark-resight part has undergone a major overhaul for the next version, expected in a few weeks), (ii) problems with small samples, or (iii) some error in the way you’ve set things up. Maybe all three.

I can at least provide some demo data files for secr-markresight.pdf (attached - they're just simulated, and may not be the same as used in the vignette). However, I would strongly advise that you hold off on analysing all-sighting data in secr 2.10, given that secr 3.0 is just around the corner (it’s coming first in pre-release form on the Density website).

I’ve a few other pedantic and dismal comments that won’t necessarily help, but here they are anyway:

1. Although in your mind you sampled grids of 36 squares, in practice what you did was to position cameras at points (perhaps at the centres or randomly within each square?). There is no real sense in which the area sampled was 9 sq km. There will be a convex polygon enclosing the outermost cameras, with area < 9 sq km, and another, unknown, area from which cows wandered in front of a camera.

2. I imagine you treated each day as a sampling occasion. That is excessive and slows things down unnecessarily. You can probably collapse all occasions down to 1 and use a ‘count’ detector type (preferably with detectfb = ‘HHN’), without losing information.

3. If you aim for an average density over all three grids then be sure to include a dummy line for Grid 2 in the capture file (using code ‘NONE’ for the animalID; see ?read.capthist).

4. It would help to have some hints regarding the extent of movements by individual cows, and whether they really move in herds (that clashes with a basic SECR assumption of independence, and probably means you have even less data than you thought).

5. Mark-resight is really no fun. Formally incorporating counts of sightings of unidentifiable cows requires that they are counted exactly as if they were identifiable – i.e. with equal probability of detection. My sense is that this is almost impossible to achieve (avoiding double counting etc.).

My suggestion is to do a standard SECR (not mark-resight) analysis of the data on identifiable animals and in your text apply an ad-hoc adjustment for the fraction of individuals that were identifiable – probably that’s what you meant to do anyway. If nothing else, the SECR analysis will give a clean estimate of sigma (if sigma large (>1km) or poorly estimated, further digging is a waste of time).

Murray

messages.subject_clean: AIC comparison ; conditional or full likelihood when looking at sex differences
messages.body_plain:
Hi Elsa,
You can compare AIC values across models fitted with either likelihood, jut not across models that use different likelihoods.
If you use the conditional likelihood (CL = T), you can't model variation in density (except possibly across sessions). It's faster, and you can model sex as an individual covariate.
If you want to use the full likelihood, you can still fit models with sex effects, by modeling the different sexes as "groups" or "sessions".

Good luck,
Eric

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michelle
I'm not clear on the missing years: presumably there was no sampling effort in those years? If so then there was no relevant trap file and it is not appropriate to include a dummy row ('NONE') in the capture file*. I understand that you are concerned to allow for the spacing of sampling years when fitting the trend model; for that you should provide a session covariate (argument 'sessioncov', one row per session, in order). Something like this should work
secr.fit(SC_CH, ..., sessioncov=data.frame(year = c(2006,2007,2010,2011,2012,2013,2015,2016)), model = D~year)
Multiple year-specific masks can be provided as a list, one component per year. Better documentation is coming!
Murray

* I think your example might fail anyway because there were only 3 columns in those years.
